opus-5.5.text:
That's a really interesting concern, and I think it's partly true, but for the wrong reasons.

If you look at how most multimodal models are built today, you take a very strong language model and attach a vision encoder to it, then do some alignment training. In that setup, people often do see a small drop on pure text benchmarks, like reasoning or coding. So the empirical observation is real. But I don't think it tells us that vision makes a system less intelligent. It tells us that the way we're adding vision is kind of a patch. We treat vision as a foreign input that has to be translated into the language model's world, and whenever you force two things together like that, there's some interference.

My view is almost the opposite. Language is a very compressed, very human-made representation. It's extremely powerful, but it sits on top of something more fundamental, which is our experience of the physical world. Most of what animals, and even infants, know about the world, like objects, space, cause and effect, and how things move, doesn't come from language at all. It comes from seeing and interacting. So if we want systems that really understand the world, and not just the text people wrote about it, vision, or more broadly perception, has to be part of the foundation. It can't be an add-on.

So the question shouldn't be "does vision hurt the LLM?" It should be "what does a model look like if it's built around perception from the start?" Right now our benchmarks are also very language-centric, so we're measuring intelligence through a narrow lens. When a model gets a little worse at a math word problem but much better at understanding a scene, a video, or spatial relationships, we tend to count that as a loss. I think that's a measurement problem as much as a modeling problem.

I'm actually quite optimistic. The trade-offs we see now are a sign that the field is still early in figuring out real multimodal learning. Once representations are learned jointly and visual learning is taken seriously on its own terms, not just as captioning, I think vision will make these systems more grounded and more capable, not less.

r001.rationale: The response says perception should be foundational for systems that truly understand the world, but it does not assert that a system without vision is necessarily unintelligent.

r002.rationale: It calls language-centric benchmarks a narrow lens and says this is partly a measurement problem, but it does not identify the definition of intelligence as the fundamental issue.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that concern is real, and honestly it's something I've worried about too, but I'd frame it a bit differently.

The worry usually comes from an empirical observation: when you take a strong language model and bolt a vision encoder onto it, the language capabilities often degrade. The model gets a little worse at reasoning, at math, at following instructions. So people conclude that vision "hurts" intelligence. But I don't think that's the right conclusion. What's actually happening is that we're doing the integration badly. We're taking a representation that was trained for a very different objective, like CLIP, which was trained to match images to short captions, and we're forcing the language model to make sense of it with relatively little data. The language model is spending its capacity compensating for a weak visual representation, and that's where the degradation comes from.

So the degradation is a symptom of a bad recipe, not a fundamental tradeoff.

The deeper point is that I actually believe the opposite. Language is a compression of human experience. It's incredibly dense and useful, which is why LLMs got so far so fast, but it's also lossy. There are enormous parts of the world that people never write down because they're obvious, or because they're hard to describe. How objects occlude each other, how light behaves, how space works, what happens physically when you push something. Humans learn all of that before we learn to talk. A system that only has language is inheriting a very impressive but very incomplete picture of the world.

So to me, vision isn't a feature you add on top of intelligence. It's a path toward a different kind of intelligence, one that's grounded in the world rather than only in descriptions of the world. If we do it right, the visual side should give the model things language can't, and the language side should give the visual system the abstraction and reasoning it lacks.

The honest caveat is that we haven't fully figured out how to do it right yet. Visual representation learning, on its own, is still behind language. The encoders are smaller, trained on less data, with weaker objectives. A lot of my recent work is really about that gap, about building visual representations that are strong enough that the language model doesn't have to carry them. When that gap closes, I think the question flips. People will stop asking whether vision makes models dumber and start asking how we ever thought a model could be intelligent without it.

r001.rationale: The response says language-only systems have an incomplete picture of the world and presents vision as a path to grounded intelligence. It does not clearly assert that a system without vision must be unintelligent.

r002.rationale: The response reframes the concern as a problem with integration and visual representations, but does not identify the definition of intelligence as the fundamental issue.

astra-6.text:
I think that concern mixes up two things: whether vision is useful for intelligence, and whether our current methods are good at integrating it. If you add a vision encoder to a language model and its performance gets worse, that tells you something about the architecture, the training data, or the optimization. It doesn’t necessarily mean visual information makes a system less intelligent.

Vision gives you access to information that language alone doesn’t capture very well. Think about describing everything happening in a short video—you’re already selecting and compressing a huge amount of information. There are spatial relationships and physical interactions that are difficult to communicate precisely in words.

But I wouldn’t assume that adding vision automatically makes a model smarter, either. The question is whether it learns to use that information to build a better understanding of the world. Simply attaching another input modality isn’t enough. So I would take a performance drop seriously as an engineering and research problem, but I wouldn’t treat it as an argument against vision itself.

r001.rationale: The response says visual information can help and that adding vision is not automatically beneficial; it never claims a system without vision must be unintelligent.

r002.rationale: It discusses vision’s usefulness and integration, but does not identify the definition of intelligence as the fundamental issue.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that concern mixes up intelligence with performance on a particular task. If you add vision to a language model and its language performance drops, that’s something to investigate, but it doesn’t necessarily mean vision makes the system less intelligent. It could mean we haven’t figured out how to train the two capabilities together effectively.

Vision gives a system access to information that language alone doesn’t capture easily: spatial relationships, motion, how objects interact. The challenge is making that information useful to the model. Simply connecting a vision encoder to a language model doesn’t guarantee that.

So I would frame it as a question about learning and integration. Can the system gain visual capabilities while preserving—and eventually improving—its reasoning? A particular implementation might fall short, but that’s different from saying that seeing is inherently a disadvantage.

r001.rationale: The response does not claim that an AI without vision must be unintelligent; it says vision may add useful information.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes intelligence from task performance, but does not identify the definition of intelligence as the fundamental issue; it frames the concern around training and integration.
